slides.text: For each number, find the first bigger number to its right: [2, 1, 5, 3]. Checking to the right of every number is O(n²).
slides.alt: nums 2, 1, 5, 3 at i = 0 to 3 above an answer row of four −1s, an empty stack, and the tag "check right of each: O(n²)".

slides.text: once someone tall stands in front of you, everyone shorter behind them is blocked for good. Only taller people ever matter again.
slides.alt: "A concert crowd": figures of different heights in a row. Someone tall in front: everyone shorter behind them is blocked. Only taller people ever matter again.
nums with 5 ringed; the answer row now reads 5, 5, −1, −1 and the stack holds 5 (i = 2).

slides.text: 3 arrives → push. At the end, 5 and 3 keep −1.
slides.alt: The answer row 5, 5, −1, −1 with "no greater → −1" under the last two; the stack holds 5 (i = 2) and 3 (i = 3).

slides.text: while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x: answer[stack.pop()] = x
slides.alt: Python next_greater(nums): answer = [-1] * len(nums); stack = []; for i, x in enumerate(nums): while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x: answer[stack.pop()] = x; stack.append(i). The pop line is highlighted with the note "…pop it: x is its answer"; the stage shows 5 > 2: pop 0, answer[0] = 5.

slides.text: Each index goes in once and comes out at most once: O(n). Our test run on 10,000 numbers (Python): 953 ms checking right of each vs 0.6 ms with the stack.
slides.alt: "10,000 numbers, our test run, Python": checking right of every number takes 953 ms; the monotonic stack takes 0.6 ms.

slides.text: The trap: store values instead of indexes, and when you pop you don't know where the answer goes.
slides.alt: "The trap: values, not indexes": stack.append(x) and answer[nums.index(stack.pop())] = x. Popped a value: where does its answer go? [1, 1, 3] → [3, −1, −1] ✗, because index(1) finds the first 1 twice and the second 1 never gets its 3.
